questions.statement: Which part of an argumentative essay clearly states your position on the topic?
questions.context: Students at Liceo Nacional de Cartago write a five-paragraph argumentative essay.

options.text: The thesis statement
options.feedback: A thesis statement declares the writer's position and argument in one clear sentence, usually at the end of the intro.

options.text: A body paragraph
options.feedback: A body paragraph develops reasons and evidence to prove that thesis, so it states the position only indirectly.

options.text: The conclusion
options.feedback: The conclusion sums up the arguments and leaves the reader with the final message, not the first claim.

options.text: A counterargument sentence
options.feedback: A counterargument sentence concedes the opposing view so the writer can answer it later in the essay.

questions.explanation:
An argumentative essay has introduction with thesis, body paragraphs, counterargument, and conclusion.

---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sentence introduces a counterargument in an essay?
questions.context: In San Jose, a student argues that the city should add more bicycle lanes.

options.text: Bicycle lanes would make traffic safer and faster for everyone.
options.feedback: This is a supporting reason for the writer's own position, so it belongs in a body paragraph, not a counterargument.

options.text: In conclusion, San Jose should build more bicycle lanes.
options.feedback: The phrase 'In conclusion' marks a closing move, so this sentence summarizes the argument instead of opposing it.

options.text: Some drivers argue that bike lanes take too much road space.
options.feedback: This sentence voices the opposing side's view, which is exactly what a counterargument does before the writer answers it.

options.text: My essay discusses bike lanes, safety and road space.
options.feedback: This sentence only names the parts of the essay, so it takes no side and cannot present an opposing view.

questions.explanation:
A counterargument states the strongest opposing claim, and the writer then refutes it to strengthen the thesis.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which thesis is clear, arguable and specific enough for that essay?
questions.context: A Heredia student wants to argue that homework in high school should be reduced.

options.text: Homework is something that students have.
options.feedback: It names a topic but states no position, so the reader cannot tell what the writer wants to prove.

options.text: High schools in Costa Rica should cut homework because it reduces sleep and motivation.
options.feedback: It takes a clear position, names a reason, and is arguable, so it works as a thesis for a persuasive essay.

options.text: Some students do not like homework.
options.feedback: This reports a vague group feeling without an arguable claim, so it cannot guide body paragraphs.

options.text: This essay will talk about homework and schools.
options.feedback: This announces the topic instead of arguing a position, which makes it a topic sentence, not a thesis.

questions.explanation:
A strong thesis takes a clear stance on a debatable issue and hints at the reasons, not only the topic.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: In an argumentative essay, what does the last sentence of the introduction do?
questions.context: In Alajuela, a student argues that the city should fund more bicycle lanes.

options.text: It gives statistics about the city.
options.feedback: Statistics belong in body paragraphs as evidence, not as the closing move of an introduction.

options.text: It lists every paragraph of the essay.
options.feedback: Outlining the paragraphs previews the structure, but an introduction ends with the position, not a list.

options.text: It answers the strongest opposing view.
options.feedback: Answering the opposing view happens in the body, after the thesis is already on the table.

options.text: It presents the thesis statement.
options.feedback: Introductions move from background to the writer's claim, so the thesis closes the paragraph and guides the body.

questions.explanation:
The introduction funnels from context to the thesis, and the thesis sentence anchors every body paragraph.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which thesis best answers the prompt about free fares on city buses?
questions.context: A student from Alajuela must defend one position about public transport in an essay.

options.text: Free bus fares in Alajuela would boost ridership and cut traffic, so the city should test them.
options.feedback: It answers the prompt directly, takes a side, and gives a reason, which is what an effective thesis must do.

options.text: Buses in Alajuela have fares and routes.
options.feedback: This only states a fact about fares, so it leaves no argument for the reader to follow or disagree with.

options.text: Fares are free in some cities.
options.feedback: This is a fact about other cities, not a position on Alajuela, so the prompt is never really addressed.

options.text: People in Alajuela can take the bus.
options.feedback: This describes a service, not an opinion, so it cannot serve as the thesis of an argumentative essay.

questions.explanation:
Answering the prompt matters as much as taking a stance: the thesis must cover the exact issue that was asked.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which thesis would be the strongest for that essay?
questions.context: A Monteverde student argues that tourism businesses should pay a local conservation fee.

options.text: Tourism is very important for Monteverde.
options.feedback: This is a fact about an industry, so it offers no position for the writer to defend or a reader to reject.

options.text: Monteverde hotels should fund reforestation, since tourism depends on the cloud forest.
options.feedback: It names who should act, what they should do, and why it matters, which makes the thesis specific and arguable.

options.text: Many people visit Monteverde every year.
options.feedback: This is a statistic about visitors, so it belongs in body paragraphs as background, not as the claim.

options.text: My favourite place in Costa Rica is Monteverde.
options.feedback: A personal preference cannot be argued with reasons and evidence, so it cannot serve as a thesis.

questions.explanation:
A thesis names the actors, the action proposed and the reason behind it, not only the subject of the essay.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Why is this body sentence weak: 'Vegetarian meals are good for everyone'?
questions.context: A Cartago student argues that the canteen should offer more vegetarian meals.

options.text: It uses the word 'good', but key words are always allowed in essays.
options.feedback: Key words from the prompt are welcome in a thesis, so the problem here is not the choice of words.

options.text: It is a short sentence, and short sentences weaken an argument.
options.feedback: Sentence length has no effect on argument quality; a short claim simply needs supporting evidence after it.

options.text: It repeats the idea of the topic sentence instead of giving proof.
options.feedback: This restates the paragraph's point in new words, so it adds no reason, example or statistic to prove it.

options.text: It is too informal because it uses the word 'everyone'.
options.feedback: The word 'everyone' is common in student writing; the real problem is that the sentence claims no evidence.

questions.explanation:
Body sentences must prove the topic sentence with facts, examples or reasons; restating the claim proves nothing.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sentence belongs in the counterargument paragraph, not the body?
questions.context: A student in Puntarenas argues that buses should run later at night for ferry workers.

options.text: Some residents say the extra night buses would increase noise complaints.
options.feedback: This reports what an opposing group believes, which is the material a counterargument paragraph refutes.

options.text: Night workers currently wait up to two hours for the last bus home.
options.feedback: This is evidence for the writer's own claim, so it belongs in a body paragraph supporting the thesis.

options.text: The city has run three different bus schedules in the last year.
options.feedback: This is a neutral fact about the city's history, so it explains the topic without arguing either side.

options.text: Later night service is exactly what ferry workers have asked the city for.
options.feedback: This restates the thesis with a source, so it strengthens the writer's position instead of opposing it.

questions.explanation:
A counterargument paragraph presents the other side's claim and then answers it, unlike body paragraphs that back your own thesis.

---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which closing sentence best finishes that argumentative essay?
questions.context: A Heredia student argues that homework should be cut in favour of sports practice.

options.text: In this essay I talked about homework, sports and school.
options.feedback: This only lists the sections of the essay, so it is a summary of the structure and not a persuasive ending.

options.text: Homework and sports are both important things in school life.
options.feedback: This is a general observation about two topics, so it adds no argument and simply restates what is already clear.

options.text: Schools that cut homework now give students back the hours that training and rest require.
options.feedback: It returns to the thesis and extends it with a consequence, which is what a strong conclusion should do.

options.text: I really liked writing about this topic for my essay.
options.feedback: This comments on the writer's own writing, not on the topic, so it tells the reader nothing new.

questions.explanation:
A good conclusion restates the claim and adds a consequence, a recommendation or a new idea rather than repeating the intro.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which evidence best supports the claim that more shade trees are needed?
questions.context: A Liberia student argues for more shade trees around the school playground.

options.text: Trees are nice and everybody likes them.
options.feedback: This is a general opinion with no evidence, so it shows the writer's taste rather than proving the need.

options.text: The school nurse counted 30 students treated for heat headaches last term.
options.feedback: Specific measured data from the school itself supports the claim and can be checked by the reader.

options.text: Trees grow in many parts of Costa Rica.
options.feedback: This only states where trees can grow, so it says nothing about conditions on this playground.

options.text: My friend says the playground feels hot at noon.
options.feedback: One friend's impression is anecdotal and unverified, so it is far weaker than recorded data.

questions.explanation:
Strong evidence is specific, measurable and checkable; opinions and single impressions prove nothing to a critical reader.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sentence best states the opposing view in this essay?
questions.context: A student in San Jose argues that recycling bins should be added to every classroom.

options.text: Recycling bins should be added to every classroom.
options.feedback: This is the writer's own thesis, so it belongs in the introduction and not with the opposing position.

options.text: Recycling protects the environment for future generations.
options.feedback: This supports the thesis with a benefit, so it serves as a body paragraph reason rather than a counter claim.

options.text: Some teachers argue that bins in classrooms create more mess than they solve.
options.feedback: It names who disagrees and what they believe, which is precisely what the counterargument paragraph must present.

options.text: In conclusion, schools should teach recycling from primary school.
options.feedback: A closing statement like 'In conclusion' belongs at the end, so this sentence cannot open the opposing argument.

questions.explanation:
A counterargument sentence attributes a claim to the other side and then answers it, which keeps the reader's trust.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which choice turns this vague claim into a debatable thesis?
questions.context: A Turrialba student argues that the town should build a public bike repair station.

options.text: Bikes help people in Turrialba get around town faster.
options.feedback: This is a general true statement, so it gives the writer nothing to argue about and readers nothing to dispute.

options.text: Public bicycle repair stations exist in many cities.
options.feedback: This is a fact about other cities, so it gives context but takes no position on what Turrialba should do.

options.text: Turrialba should build a public bike repair station near the main park.
options.feedback: It states a clear proposal about a specific place, so readers can agree or disagree and the essay has a real question.

options.text: My cousin rides a bicycle to work every morning.
options.feedback: A single personal habit is an anecdote, not an arguable position that a whole essay could defend.

questions.explanation:
A thesis is arguable when readers could reasonably disagree, so it must propose something instead of stating a fact.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which option repairs this flaw in the thesis 'School is not perfect for us'?
questions.context: A student in Puntarenas argues that school start times should be later.

options.text: School is not perfect for anybody anywhere in the world.
options.feedback: Adding 'anywhere in the world' keeps the claim vague, so the writer still avoids naming who should act.

options.text: School is not perfect, and that is fine.
options.feedback: Adding 'and that is fine' turns the complaint into agreement, so the thesis no longer argues for a change.

options.text: School is the most perfect system that was ever built.
options.feedback: Calling school the most perfect system contradicts the critical tone and drops the argument about start times.

options.text: Costa Rican high schools should start at 7:30 a.m. so students get more sleep.
options.feedback: It adds a specific actor, a concrete proposal and a reason, which turns a complaint into a defensible thesis.

questions.explanation:
A thesis needs a specific proposal plus a reason; vague complaints about a system cannot be argued for or against.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which paragraph would most weaken the argument that water data should be public?
questions.context: A student in Tibas writes an essay arguing that the municipality should publish water quality reports.

options.text: Only three families in Tibas read the newspaper, so reports reach few people.
options.feedback: A small readership may limit impact, but it does not remove the public's right to know how their water is treated.

options.text: The ministry already publishes national water data every year, so local reports would add nothing.
options.feedback: Existing national data makes the local proposal redundant, which removes the writer's reason for asking for change.

options.text: Water quality in Tibas has improved since the treatment plant was rebuilt.
options.feedback: Improved quality supports the writer's concern and shows the system works, so it strengthens rather than weakens it.

options.text: Reading about water takes time that students would rather spend playing sports.
options.feedback: Saying people prefer other activities criticises their choices instead of the argument, so it is not a real objection.

questions.explanation:
A strong objection attacks the necessity or logic of the proposal, not the habits or preferences of the people involved.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which reply most convincingly refutes the objection about cost?
questions.context: A student in Liberia argues that the canton should replace diesel buses with electric ones.

options.text: Electric buses cost nothing, so the cost objection is simply false.
options.feedback: Saying the cost is zero is factually untrue, so this reply loses credibility instead of answering the objection.

options.text: The canton should think about money more carefully before buying anything new.
options.feedback: This asks readers to agree on tone rather than reasons, so it offers no evidence to settle the money question.

options.text: Over ten years the lower fuel and maintenance costs repay the price, plus grants cover part of it.
options.feedback: It answers with a time frame, comparable costs and funding, so it meets the objection with evidence rather than slogans.

options.text: Diesel buses are the cheapest option, so the canton should keep them.
options.feedback: Restating the objection as the writer's conclusion abandons the thesis, so the argument collapses instead of being defended.

questions.explanation:
To refute an objection you must answer the same point with data or reasoning, not change the subject or drop your thesis.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which plan best answers this prompt about a protected bike lane in Alajuela?
questions.context: A student in Alajuela argues that the town should build a protected bike lane network.

options.text: This essay will describe the history of bicycles in Alajuela.
options.feedback: Announcing a history is only a topic, so the plan never commits to a position the reader could debate.

options.text: In this essay I will discuss my favourite bike and where I ride it.
options.feedback: Focusing on a private favourite narrows the essay to the writer, so it cannot persuade the whole community.

options.text: The word bike comes from English and refers to a two-wheeled vehicle.
options.feedback: Defining the word 'bike' is a vocabulary step, so it prepares no argument at all about the town's transport.

options.text: This essay argues that Alajuela should build protected bike lanes and refutes the cost objection.
options.feedback: It names the stance and the objection to answer, which is exactly what an argumentative essay plan must promise.

questions.explanation:
An argumentative plan states the position plus the arguments and objections, while a narrative or descriptive plan would not.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which revised sentence turns this weak claim into a strong argumentative thesis?
questions.context: A Monteverde student argues that eco-tour operators should limit daily visitor numbers.

options.text: Tourists should think about nature when they visit cloud forests.
options.feedback: This is gentle advice with no proposal, so there is nothing for readers to support or reject in the essay.

options.text: Reserving cloud forest trails will protect fragile habitats and keep local guides employed.
options.feedback: It proposes one action and gives two benefits, so it is specific, arguable and supported by the paragraphs to follow.

options.text: Monteverde is a beautiful place that many tourists like to visit.
options.feedback: A compliment to the destination supports neither side of the debate, so it cannot carry an argumentative thesis.

options.text: The trail system was built a long time ago and it is still used today.
options.feedback: This historical note gives background context, which belongs in the introduction rather than in the thesis itself.

questions.explanation:
A strong thesis proposes a specific action and adds a reason, so the essay can spend its paragraphs proving that benefit.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sentence belongs in the introduction rather than the body?
questions.context: A student in Heredia argues that public libraries should stay open on Sundays.

options.text: Last year 4,300 people borrowed books on Saturdays.
options.feedback: A yearly borrowing figure is evidence, so it belongs in a body paragraph that supports the thesis.

options.text: Students who work weekends lose all library access during the week.
options.feedback: This explains who loses access and why, so it works as a body reason that justifies the thesis.

options.text: Libraries in Heredia should remain open on Sundays so working students can study.
options.feedback: It states the position the whole essay defends, which is the thesis sentence that opens the introduction.

options.text: Some people prefer buying books in a shop instead of borrowing them.
options.feedback: This reports an opposing preference, so it belongs in the counterargument paragraph, not the introduction.

questions.explanation:
The introduction states the claim and hints at the reasons; the body then proves them with evidence one at a time.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which reason would be most convincing inside a body paragraph?
questions.context: A Cartago student argues that the university should offer more evening classes.

options.text: Two thousand students work in the morning, so evening classes would let them keep studying.
options.feedback: It links a measurable group to a specific benefit, so the reason is relevant, checkable and supports the thesis.

options.text: Evening classes sound nice and would probably be fun.
options.feedback: A pleasant impression with 'probably' shows taste and doubt, so it proves nothing about student needs.

options.text: The university has been the same for a long time.
options.feedback: Pointing out that the university is old adds nothing to the case for new evening timetables.

options.text: I would like evening classes for my own convenience.
options.feedback: Personal convenience is a narrow motive and it ignores the wider benefit the essay claims for other students.

questions.explanation:
A convincing body reason answers 'so what' with facts, numbers or causes that matter to the people affected.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which evidence is strongest for the claim that plastic bottles waste water?
questions.context: A student in Guapiles argues that the school should replace drinking fountains with bottle fillers.

options.text: Students prefer cold water from fountains over warm tap water.
options.feedback: This describes a preference, so it says nothing measurable about how much water the two systems consume.

options.text: Bottle fillers are a modern idea that some schools already use.
options.feedback: This proves that the idea exists elsewhere, but it gives no figure about water use in this school.

options.text: Cleaning one fountain and refilling a bottle uses about eight times less water than washing a new bottle.
options.feedback: The general remark offers no data, so a reader cannot judge whether bottles really waste water.

options.text: Plastic bottles are everywhere in the world today.
options.feedback: It compares quantified water use for both systems, so readers can verify the claim and accept it.

questions.explanation:
Comparative figures that contrast two options turn a general claim into evidence a reader can check.
